content.title: Authors' Response
content.comment:
Dear AC and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank the AC and Reviewers for their constructive comments and helpful suggestions.

We sincerely appreciate the positive comments, such as "important problem", "interesting idea",  and "clear motivation". Also, most reviewers showed their interests in future extension of this paper, especially in the direction of deeper networks. These are very encouraging.

At the same time, reviewers also raise concerns on the presentation. Please accept our apologizes on this. We will definitely revise our paper to ensure clarity and readability.

Unfortunately, the limited time of the rebuttal session is not enough for us to extend our theory and revise this paper. Thus, we decide to withdraw this paper, carefully revise it, explore in wider domains, and prepare for the next venue.

Thanks again for your time and feedback. Very much appreciated.

Best regards,

The Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper introduces the term "intrinsic computational complexity" which is the computational complexity of a neural network which takes into account that collinear channels can be combined into one operation. The authors then compare three neural networks: a standard network, an equivariant network and an equivariant network with group-averaging. The authors prove three theorems which set relations between these networks in terms of their expressive power and intrinsic computational complexity
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper considers an interesting observation and builds a theory around it. However, I found it very complicated to follow the story of the paper. I am absolutely sure that a paper which focuses on the relation between standard networks and group-equivariant counterparts is and will be of high interest to the community. The current version of the manuscript requires significant modifications. 

I didn't fully understand the motivation of the authors until I read the paragraph "Intrinsic computational complexity." at the very bottom of page 4. Thus the first 4 pages look almost irrelevant until this point. After reading the paragraph I reconsidered the previous pages and found them insightful. I thus suggest the authors to change the order of the paragraphs and start with the main point of the motivation. As a person interested in efficient implementation of group-equivariant CNNs, I found this motivation significant.

There are several issues, which affect my rating
1. Will your thereoms work for deeper neural networks? How would the proofs look like in these cases? If the claims are only true for 2 layer neural networks, then what is the possible generalization of such claims to deeper nets?
2. Will the theorems work for the most common group - the translation group? Will they work for the 2D scaling group?
3. Does the results of the theorems depend on the type of representations which are used? For example, let us consider an E(2) equivariant neural network. We can construct it by using irreps, or we can cosider a P4 subgroup and base the implementation on regular representations. What will change in the theorems?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper seems clear only after several iterations of jumping back and forth. I suppose it may be fixed and thus, I would like to pay the authors attention to this problem.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents an interesting idea, however, it is hard to follow and lacks some important points.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the computational costs at inference, theoretical ("intrinsic") and empirical, for equivariant networks and group equivariant networks of some desired expressivity. The results are also compared with MLPs without any equivariance constraints. The authors define, what they call "intrinsic complexity" for this purpose. It is shown that for 2-layer equivariant networks (TENs) and graph averaging networks (TGNs), the intrinsic complexity can be twice that of an ordinary MLP. At the same time, TEN and TGN have similar intrinsic complexities. Further, it is shown that TENs can achieve a similar complexity empirically, while TGNs are strictly slower.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
> Strengths:
- Understanding the complexity inherent in the training and evaluation of GCNNs is an important problem to study, and largely unexplored. The paper has good motivation, focusing on inference.

> Weaknesses:
- The paper needs a thorough rewrite. It seems to have a lot of typos and grammatical errors throughout. Further, many terms are used incorrectly, or not defined at all, which often makes it unclear what the authors want to say, and one needs to go back and forth to guess what might be meant. Let me give two examples: 
1. The authors talk about the "group scale" starting from the abstract. In the first paragraph too, there are statements such as "the group can have a scale up to 1000", but the notion of "group scale" is never defined -- and such terminology to my knowledge is not standard. Reading on, it becomes clear around page 4 what they might mean. But it would be useful to clarify at the onset what is meant. Since this is not the case, the motivation appears a bit shaky. 
2. Similar to the above, again in the intro., are statements such as "merges the inner product operations between the same-direction channel weight vectors and the input vector". One might assume that it is informal usage for the intro., but then it repeats in the technical section as well. What do the authors mean by "same-direction vectors"? Again, like the above, it takes a while to read to take a guess at what might be meant, and a seeming definition appears in page 5 -- which seems overtly restrictive. This already puts the paper in a weak spot. 

- The problem, however, is not just restricted to writing and grammar. It is often not clear what the authors are trying to convey. For instance, there seems to be an indexing error in section 4.1 both when they define a NN and towards the end of the section. If it is indeed correct, it seems a bit odd to me -- because it is first defined as a vector, and then the indexing is over separate vectors. Do the authors mean separate channels? (as it seems to be the case). Nevertheless, moving on, the authors then claim that if the channels have the same weights, the computation is repeated and needs to be merged, and the complexity of this merged unit is called "intrinsic complexity". Sure, a repetition of weight vectors leads to wasted computation. But it is not clear to me how this kind of a notion captures "complexity" appropriately -- shouldn't one be looking at the degree of independence or something of the weight vector instead to arrive at something more useful? In any case, if the channel weights are indeed the same, this can easily be adjusted in a re-designed network. I am not quite sure I follow how this is an interesting quantity vis-a-vis GCNNs. I would have expected to see something along the lines of the size of the intertwiner space, and how that changes the inherent complexity that a GCNN needs. 

- Using the quantity defined above, section 4.2 has two theorems that show that TGNs and TENs have the same intrinsic complexity. This amounts to doing the merger above and computing said quantity. Again I don't know how the algebraic structure comes into play, apart from a simple way. The next result goes on to say that the intrinsic complexity of TENs and TGNs will be at most 2 times the complexity of TNs. This is shown by an example -- which I don't quite understand how it generalizes. Since we are talking about complexity, a lower bound is of greater interest. But from the framework and quantity defined, I am not sure if it would be meaningful. 

- Section 4.5 has a no-free lunch theorem which on the surface sounds reasonable. But the problem is that the notion of scale is never defined properly. Second, the use of "correlation" implies that we are dealing with some random quantities, which I never see defined either. So while on the surface it seems intuitive to me (if I plug in some notions by myself), I am actually not sure what the statement intends to convey. 


> Minor comments: 

There are many typos etc., throughout. Some examples are below:

- Typo, Abstract: "two-layer networks without any equivariant constraints" --> two-layer networks without any equivariance constraints

- Abstract: "TGNs/TENs have equal and full expressivities" I think using expressivity is better

- Abstract: "where the TGNs and TENs have equal intrinsic computational complexities" same as above. 

- Preliminaries: The general linear group is referred to as the "isomorphism group" at some point. I am not sure this is standard terminology. 

- Preliminaries: "permutates" should be permutes

- Preliminaries: "permutating" should be permuting. 

- End of page 4: "the discrepancy aforementioned is rectified" --> the aforementioned discrepancy...

- The notion of "intrinsic" symmetry is not used in the literature as used in the paper. It so happens that it doesn't matter here. But when we are talking of, for instance, invariance under rigid transformations and possibly scaling, we are talking about "extrinsic" symmetry.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has serious issues with clarity. Many quantities are never defined and are sometimes used in different ways. Since a lot of the writing is not very precise, it is not clear to me what to make of some of the results. I think the authors also fail to first convey a sense of why the quantity that they study is of relevance to practical GCNNs. Considering the same channels weights to somehow define an "intrinsic' notion of complexity also doesn't seem well motivated. Seeing a paper on complexity, one might expect some kind of lower and upper bound based on the "dimension" of a group (number of dimensions required such that a representation can be faithful), compared to an MLP. But that will require an appeal to Fourier analysis and various sampling theorems. In general, to give a flavour, even the question that whether FFTs of many groups of interest in ML are even possible remains open. I understand that the authors are only looking at inference, but then the quantity that they study needs additional motivation and related to practical GCNNs, perhaps by giving examples in the beginning.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper shows two alternative (and equivalent) constructions for two-layer equivariant networks with ReLU non-linearity, and argues about the computational complexity of equiavariant networks based on these constructions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths

Clear motivation for the main result/overall theoretical contributions.

Clear equivalence construction between an arbitrary equivariant network and two more theoretically tractable objects.

### Weaknesses

The most interesting results (no-free-lunch, Th. 4.7) lacks decent explanation/formal proof.

No discussion on deeper networks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity

Overall the paper is well-written, but some parts could be improved:

Sec. 4.1 onwards: I’d use a different letter for \sigma_i as \sigma is used for non-linearity.

It’s worth numbering some/all equations. 

Equation before Def. 4.1: I’d say it’s worth reminding \sigma is ReLU. Although the expression should work for any homogeneous function (with some scaling changes).

4 lines above Def. 4.1: \sigma missing in the sum

Theorem 4.4. Suppose a TN is -of- an (remove of)

Sec. 4.5:  nonlinearity ReLU -> ReLU nonlinearity

### Quality 

Questions/concern 1: are the two paragraphs after Th. 4.7 the proof of that theorem? If not, I couldn’t find it. If yes, it should be written down in more details, as it seems to be the most interesting part of the paper. Right now the equivalence constructions seem interesting but they don't immediately support the main claim, i.e. the no-free-lunch theorem.

Question 2: It seems that all results hold true for any 1-homogeneous function ($f(s\mathbf{x})=sf(\mathbf{x})$), not just ReLU. Is that correct? Can they also be extended for any $\lambda$-homogeneous function ($f(s\mathbf{x})=s^\lambda f(\mathbf{x})$)?

### Novelty
To my knowledge the work is novel.

### Reproducibility
Theory only.

content.title: Intrinsic Computational Complexity of Equivariant Neural Networks
content.abstract: Equivariant neural networks have shown significant advantages in learning on data with intrinsic symmetries represented by groups. A major concern is on the high computational costs in the cases of large-scale groups, especially in the inference stage. This paper studies the required computational complexity of equivariant neural networks in inference for achieving a desired expressivity. We theoretically compare three classes of ReLU networks: (1) two-layer group-averaging networks (TGNs); (2) two-layer layer-wise equivariant networks (TENs); and (3) two-layer networks without any equivariant constraints (TNs), with a new notion {\it intrinsic computational complexity} for better characterizing computational costs. We prove that (1) TGNs/TENs have equal and full expressivities to represent any invariant function that can be learned by a TN, where the TGNs and TENs have equal intrinsic computational complexities; (2) a TGN/TEN requires at most double the intrinsic computational complexity of a TN; and (3) a TEN can achieve the inference speed coincident with its intrinsic computational complexity, while TGNs are strictly slower, which justifies the computational advantages of layer-wise equivariant architectures over group averaging. Our theory rules out the existence of equivariant networks with group-scale-independent computational costs, summarized in a new no-free-lunch theorem: when more equivariance is desired, more computation is required.
